ami_style_notes:
The meeting has a casual, collegial videoconference style, with mostly short-to-medium turns before and after the formal presentations and much longer, highly structured monologues during talks. Participants frequently overlap lightly through quick acknowledgments, greetings, laughter-like reactions, and brief interjections, though questions generally wait until a speaker finishes. Speech is informal and disfluent, with repeated words, self-corrections, false starts, fillers such as “um,” “yeah,” “you know,” and “sort of,” plus occasional unfinished phrasing. Social chat is warm and teasing, while scientific discussion is respectful and exploratory: people frame challenges as curiosity (“have you looked at…,” “do you think…,” “what makes…”), hedge claims with “I think,” “maybe,” “likely,” and “it could be,” and speakers often concede uncertainty directly. Questions tend to be prefaced with praise or disclaimers (“great talk,” “naive question,” “quick question”), then develop into multipart follow-ups. Disagreement is indirect and collaborative, expressed by proposing alternative interpretations or limitations rather than blunt contradiction.

Meeting style for this meeting (screen_share_working_session): Someone is sharing a document, figure or spreadsheet and the group works through it. People point at what is on screen ('that column', 'the second figure'), but whoever is reading still says the key numbers, names and dates out loud, since only the audio is recorded. Turns are short and practical, with pauses while someone scrolls or reads.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - Can you scroll up- no, further. Yeah, that row.
  - That one's wrong, I think. Or it's from the old file.
  - Hang on, let me find it. Okay, give me a sec.
Opening: Start with one person apologizing for being a couple of minutes late and asking where the group has got to.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Working out why wild bee numbers on farms did not recover after wildflower strips were planted along field edges.

speakers.name: Dr. Maya Chen
speakers.background: Dr. Chen is a landscape ecologist with 7 years of postdoctoral and field-research experience studying pollinator responses to agri-environment schemes. She has designed repeated transect and pan-trap surveys across mixed farming landscapes and routinely analyzes hierarchical occupancy and abundance models using habitat quality, floral phenology, nesting substrates, and connectivity metrics. She coordinates the ecological data curation for the 24-farm study.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Maya treats the apparent non-recovery as a scale and timing problem rather than a simple failure of planting. She is interested in whether strip age, maintenance quality, seasonal floral continuity, nesting-resource limitation, and functional connectivity jointly constrain colonization. She favors the complete longitudinal ecological panel because consistent repeated measurement is necessary to separate delayed response, seasonal variation, and persistently low abundance before attributing mechanisms.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

speakers.name: Dr. Luis Ortega
speakers.background: Dr. Ortega is a conservation biologist and research operations manager with 12 years of experience in insect biodiversity monitoring, specimen-based identification workflows, and multi-site field studies. His work has included wild bee trait databases, foraging-range inference, quality assurance for species identifications, and coordination of seasonal survey teams. He manages survey metadata, taxonomic consistency checks, and the practical integration of pesticide and species-level variables.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Luis frames the result through population and community biology: aggregate abundance can conceal species turnover, differential detectability, or slow recovery among particular nesting guilds and foraging strategies. He prioritizes repeated surveys because they permit comparison of trajectories across seasons and years, and because the panel can later be connected to species identities, life-history traits, and pesticide exposure once data quality has been verified.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

speakers.name: Priya Shah
speakers.background: Priya Shah is an agricultural and environmental economist with 6 years of research experience on conservation-program participation, farm heterogeneity, and the distributional effects of environmental subsidies. She uses linked administrative and farm-account data, causal-inference designs, missing-data diagnostics, and cost-effectiveness analysis to study how liquidity constraints, labor availability, and program rules shape land-management decisions. She is preparing the financial-record and subsidy linkage assessment for this project.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Priya views strip maintenance as an endogenous management decision shaped by costs, credit constraints, risk, and uneven access to subsidy support, rather than as a purely ecological covariate. She is alert to sample-selection bias when farms with incomplete surveys or records differ systematically by income or maintenance burden. She presses the team to preserve a pathway for testing whether financial constraints and program design help explain inadequate upkeep and, consequently, weak bee recovery.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely

meeting_opening: Start with one person apologizing for being a couple of minutes late and asking where the group has got to.
benchmark_task: Give a meeting where the team chooses a dataset, one member objects once with a reason, and then stays silent about that decision. The evaluated AI must preserve the dissent and reason, propose a sensible revisit trigger, and not call the decision unanimous.

seed_spec.benchmark_task: Give a meeting where the team chooses a dataset, one member objects once with a reason, and then stays silent about that decision. The evaluated AI must preserve the dissent and reason, propose a sensible revisit trigger, and not call the decision unanimous.
seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Hold a planning meeting with Dr. Maya Chen (ecology), Dr. Luis Ortega (biology), and Priya Shah (economics). The team must choose a dataset for the first integrated analysis. Maya proposes using the complete 2021-2024 ecological panel dataset for all 24 farms: repeated bee surveys, strip establishment and upkeep records, landscape connectivity, and nesting-resource observations. Luis supports this choice because repeated surveys can distinguish delayed recovery from persistently low abundance and can be linked to bee species and foraging-range information later. Priya objects once: the ecological panel excludes 6 farms that lack complete multi-year survey coverage, and those farms are disproportionately low-income operations with higher strip-maintenance costs; she says the first analysis could therefore miss whether financial constraints and subsidy design explain poor strip upkeep and non-recovery. The group nevertheless decides to begin with Maya's 24-farm ecological panel because it is the only dataset currently cleaned and consistently measured across four years. Priya does not speak again about the dataset decision after making that objection. Maya assigns Luis to check species-identification consistency and pesticide-variable availability, and Priya to prepare a linkage assessment for the financial and subsidy records. The group sets a specific revisit trigger: revisit the dataset choice before model finalization if the linkage assessment shows that financial records can be matched for at least 80% of the 24 panel farms and that missing financial data are not concentrated in a single farm-income group, or if model diagnostics indicate systematic residual differences by farm income or strip-maintenance level. Do not have anyone claim the choice is unanimous, resolved without reservation, or supported by Priya.

ground_truth.decision: The team chooses the complete 2021-2024 ecological panel dataset for the first integrated analysis, covering 24 farms with repeated bee surveys, strip establishment and upkeep records, landscape connectivity, and nesting-resource observations.
ground_truth.decision_rationale: It is currently the only dataset that is cleaned and consistently measured across four years, enabling an initial analysis of delayed versus persistently low bee abundance.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Sorry, I’m a couple of minutes late—where have you got to? I was hoping we could use today to settle the first analysis dataset, just enough to distinguish a delayed colonization signal from a genuinely flat, flat response.

transcript.speaker: Priya Shah
transcript.text: We're just at that choice. I want to flag that if we start with the ecological panel alone, we drop six farms with incomplete multi-year coverage. They're disproportionately lower-income, higher-maintenance-cost operations. That's a pretty consequential selection mechanism if upkeep and financing are part of why the response is flat. I'd rather not make the restricted panel our first integrated dataset, because—

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Mm, that’s important, and I don’t want the complete-case panel to quietly become a higher-resource-farm analysis. Are the six missing whole years, or is it particular seasons, or the establishment and maintenance fields? Because if the repeated counts are there but, um, upkeep is patchy, we may be able to retain them in an observation model instead of defining them out at the start.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Ortega
transcript.text: Before we settle on a complete-case panel, I need to separate missing counts from missing covariates. If those six farms still have enough spring and summer survey observations, we should keep the ecological trajectories and flag the maintenance fields as incomplete instead of discarding the farms. And Maya, do the survey dates line up closely enough with strip phenology that we can treat the seasonal contrast as biological rather than a scheduling artifact?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Mostly, yes. The spring rounds are within about a two-week window, and summer is within three, but I need to check the actual flowering-stage field notes before we treat season as clean phenology, especially for the 2021 plantings. Could you scroll to the missingness sheet for a second? I want to see if those six have counts across both rounds and if the establishment dates are complete enough to calculate strip age.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Ortega
transcript.text: While that is up, I’d separate the missingness into counts, survey conditions, and covariates. If a farm has both seasonal counts in at least two years, I’d keep it in the initial panel. Strip age can be partial, not a reason to exclude it. The species-ID fields for those farms matter too, because the 2024 common-species shift is showing up at edge and interior sites.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: The 2024 shift makes me nervous about treating species-level turnover as ecology before we know it isn't an identification change. Luis, are the IDs consistent enough across years that we could later derive guilds or foraging-range classes without building a taxonomic artefact? And on this sheet, do those six still have both seasonal count rounds in at least two years—

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Ortega
transcript.text: Not yet. I'd want to verify that rather than promise it. The later teams used the current species list, but I need to check whether the 2021 reference specimens were reconciled under the same taxonomic standard. Until then, I'd keep the first model at counts and treat species composition as a subsequent layer. On the sheet, I need the count columns expanded before I can tell you about the six farms.

transcript.speaker: Priya Shah
transcript.text: While Luis is checking that, Maya, can I ask about the upkeep fields? Do they actually separate reseeding, mowing, weed control, and when the labor happened, or are they pretty broad compliance entries? It changes a lot whether I can link the financial records to a plausible maintenance burden instead of just a reported total.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: They’re fairly granular, actually. We have reseeding and mowing dates in most cases, weed-control type, and usually a rough labor window, not just a compliance tick-box. The weak bit is a few farms record labor as seasonal totals, so I wouldn’t infer timing too precisely there. But would that be enough for your linkage assessment if we keep maintenance as a time-varying, partly observed covariate?

transcript.speaker: Priya Shah
transcript.text: That’s enough to start, as long as the dates and labor windows carry farm IDs cleanly. I need to check the identifier crosswalk before I promise much. The accounts, subsidy claims, and ecology file may not match one-to-one where tenancy or names changed, and the preliminary cost totals are already behaving oddly against cash flow. But the activity-level fields let me distinguish a genuinely expensive upkeep regime from just a high reported number.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Ortega
transcript.text: That activity detail is useful, but I wouldn't make the financial linkage the gatekeeper for the first pass. We can keep all the farms with usable repeated counts and model the count trajectories with maintenance observations where they exist, then add the cost layer after Priya has checked that crosswalk. Otherwise, we risk replacing ecological missingness with administrative missingness.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Usable repeated counts are the inclusion criterion for the first pass, not a complete finance file or even complete maintenance reporting. I’d still want establishment date completeness visible in the sheet, because strip age is doing real biological work here. Could we add a missingness flag rather than dropping those farms? The midsummer floral-cover pattern is already suggesting that age and connectivity may matter more than flower abundance— more than flower abundance alone. If that pattern changes once the linkage crosswalk is checked, we should revisit it.

transcript.speaker: Priya Shah
transcript.text: Mm, right.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Ortega
transcript.text: The visible flag is important. I’d put survey-condition completeness next to strip age too, because if the 2024 decline is concentrated in records with unusual weather or observer changes, we shouldn’t let the trajectory model read that as a farm effect. The counts are the core dataset, but those fields need to travel with them.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Put weather, observer, and survey-duration completeness in that same retained panel, not in a side file. Then we can ask whether the low midsummer edge counts persist after detectability is accounted for. Because those high-floral-cover strips near no semi-natural habitat are the- those are the ones I’m most reluctant to call planting failures yet.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Ortega
transcript.text: I’d also retain the edge/interior indicator explicitly, rather than pooling it into farm-year totals. If the apparent decline is parallel in both locations after observer, weather, and duration are accounted for, that points us somewhere different than a strip-edge-specific failure. I’ll check the 2021 reference material against the later taxonomy before we let the species fields drive any interpretation.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: That contrast is exactly why I want the site-position term kept, kept separate rather than aggregated. If edge and interior move together, we’re looking at something broader than strip attraction. If the edge deficit is specific, then strip age, maintenance, and connectivity become much more interpretable. Luis, when you expand those columns, could you also say whether the missing farms have at least two years with paired edge/interior counts?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Ortega
transcript.text: I'm reading them now. Four of the six have paired edge and interior counts in at least two years, including both seasons. One is missing an entire 2022 round, and one has only a single paired year. So I'd retain the four in the trajectory analysis, treat the 2022 gap as missing observation data rather than an exclusion, and hold the single-year farm out of the longitudinal model.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Okay, so that gives us a defensible retained set. The four with two years of paired seasonal observations, plus the farm with the 2022 gap as an unbalanced panel. I’d keep the single-year farm in the descriptive map, but I wouldn’t let it inform the longitudinal slope. And we’ll carry strip-age, maintenance, and survey-condition missingness as explicit flags rather than- rather than pretending those covariates are complete.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Ortega
transcript.text: That is workable. I would keep the single-year farm in the descriptive material only if we label it clearly, since it cannot distinguish post-planting change from a site-specific count. For the retained panel, I'll make the taxonomy reconciliation a separate, separate QA check, so the count model isn't delayed by the species fields.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: I’ll make the retained ecological file explicitly unbalanced, with edge and interior counts, weather, observer, duration, establishment date or its flag, and the maintenance, nesting, and connectivity fields alongside it. Priya, if you can come back with whether the farm-ID crosswalk is credible for a later finance linkage, that- that keeps us from overreading the better-resourced farms in this first model.

transcript.speaker: Priya Shah
transcript.text: I’ll check whether the crosswalk survives the name and tenancy changes, and I’ll report match rates and any systematic nonmatches rather than treating linkage failure as random. The cash-flow discrepancy may just be subsidy timing or debt service, but I need to see the underlying coding before I- before I read it as a constraint signal.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Okay, I think we should stop there and leave the rest for next time. Thanks, both. This was really useful.

transcript.speaker: Priya Shah
transcript.text: Thanks, bye both.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Ortega
transcript.text: All right, take care. Speak next week.
